n0: Figure eight. Issue to draft PR.
n1: Now the agent writes real code. fix-issue takes a GitHub issue to a draft pull request. Before its gate, it reads and thinks. After it, it writes: a branch, commits, a push, a pull request. The gate sits on that seam.
n2: The checkout is clean, on main. Hand it the issue number.
n3: It fetched the issue, called it a feature, wrote a plan, and checked that every acceptance criterion maps to a step. Then it stopped.
n4: The plan even keeps tide times in UTC, the convention from the project notebook. Approve, and only now does any code get written.
n5: Your checkout stays safe because the run gets its own git worktree: a second working tree of the repo, on a branch named for the run. Every node runs there. It implements, runs the project's own checks, fixes what fails, and a hard gate refuses to open a PR over broken checks.
n6: Checks pass. It pushes the branch, opens the pull request, and makes sure it's a draft.
n7: Three reviewers then read the diff for correctness, conventions, and coverage, and a judge keeps only what it can confirm. Nothing needed fixing.
n8: There's no CI on this sandbox, so the PR stays a draft.
n8b: Your checkout is still main, still clean.
n8c: And the draft is waiting on GitHub.
n9: So the agent can't write before you approve, can't touch your checkout, and can't open a PR over failing checks. You review a draft, not a surprise.
n10: Read, approve, then write, somewhere else.
n11: Keelson. Lay the keel, raise the ribs.
